paper_title: Boundary-Aware Policy Learning for Agent-Orchestrated Robot Manipulation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Agent-orchestrated robot systems combine the general reasoning capability of multimodal agents with the precise physical control of learned visuomotor policies. Yet such systems often fail at the moment of handoff: a policy is reliable only from a limited set of start states, while the agent may invoke it outside this region. We call this region the policy's handoff boundary. Existing whole-task policies typically have handoff boundaries that are narrow and difficult for an agent to characterize, making reliable coordination challenging. We propose Boundary-Aware Policy Learning, which explicitly shapes and then expands the handoff boundary of a visuomotor policy. First, Boundary-Explicit Training fine-tunes the policy on contact segments with diverse start poses, yielding a wide and well-defined boundary that can be communicated to the agent through a simple handoff protocol. Second, Boundary-Expanding Self-Improvement retrains the policy on curated successful system rollouts, extending the boundary toward earlier stages of each task and allowing the agent to hand over sooner with fewer language-model calls. Across RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboDojo, our system outperforms the strongest baseline by over 26 percentage points, reaching 98.4% success in randomized RoboTwin 2.0 scenes, while further reducing its API cost and execution time by 41.3% and 37.5%, respectively. These results suggest that the key to robust agent-policy orchestration lies not only in improving either component individually, but also in explicitly shaping the boundary between them.

Introduction Robot manipulation needs both task-level decisions and precise physical interaction with objects. Agents built on general-purpose multimodal models now handle the task level through tool calls: they capture images, segment objects, plan multi-step tasks and recover when step fails [17, 26, 27, 33, 35]. Such an agent generalizes across layouts and instructions but executes contact poorly, whereas learned visuomotor policy executes contact well. Recent systems therefore combine their strengths: the agent orchestrates the task and hands over physical interaction with objects to such policy [14, 15, 32, 43, 50, 51], paradigm we refer to as agent-orchestrated robot manipulation. However, policy completes its command reliably only from limited range of states, and the agent may hand over outside this range. We refer to this range as the handoff boundary of the policy. These systems call an off-theshelf policy that is trained to complete whole tasks from initial states, which leaves this boundary narrow and hard to describe in the middle of task (Fig. 1a). As result, the agent tends to hand over the whole task from the initial pose. When the policy fails, the agent corrects the arm and hands over once more, but often from state outside the boundary, so the policy fails again, as we observe in Sec. 4.4. Existing systems mostly mitigate such failures on the agent side, through exploration, memory and verification [15, 32, 43, 51], but these measures cannot change the boundary, which is mainly set by the data on which the policy is trained. This raises natural question: Can policy be trained to have handoff boundary that is wide and explicit to the agent, for more reliable agentpolicy coordination? In this paper, we propose Boundary-Aware Policy Learning. The key idea is to define and expand the handoff boundary through training, instead of constraining the agent through prompts or letting the agent discover the boundary through exploration. In its first stage, Boundary-Explicit Training, the policy is fine-tuned only on contact segments, in which the robot physically interacts with objects. We collect these segments with diverse start poses around the target object to make the boundary wide (Fig. 1b), and the well-defined rules for collecting them make the boundary explicit. With short handoff protocol that describes this boundary, the agent calls the policy reliably. However, these reliable calls come at cost: the policy covers only the contact segment, and the agent completes the rest of each task through many slow and costly language-model calls. To reduce these calls, the second stage, Boundary-Expanding Self-Improvement, first collects the successful rollouts of entire tasks that the system produces and removes their suboptimal segments with data curation pipeline, as illustrated in Fig. 1c. We then retrain the policy on these curated rollouts together with the contact segments from the first stage, so that the handoff boundary extends to earlier stages of each task while preserving the boundary learned in the first stage. After re-exploring each task with the retrained policy, the agent hands over earlier and needs fewer language-model calls. In summary, our contributions are as follows: We propose Boundary-Aware Policy Learning, which defines and expands the handoff boundary through training, for more reliable agentpolicy coordination. To this end, we introduce Boundary-Explicit Training (Sec. 3.2), which makes the handoff boundary wide and explicit, and Boundary-Expanding Self-Improvement (Sec. 3.3), which extends it to earlier stages of each task. With boundary-explicit training alone, our system outperforms the strongest baseline by more than 26 percentage points in randomized scenes of RoboTwin 2.0 [9] and on RoboDojo [8]. On RoboTwin 2.0, self-improvement further reduces its API cost and time per episode by 41.3% and 37.5% on average, without loss in success rate (Fig. 1d). 2. Related Work Agentic robot manipulation. Language models were first used as robot planners that compose fixed set of primitives [1, 16, 17, 27]. More recently, frontier models have made it possible for an agent to control robot arm directly, with no robot-specific training [34, 45, 46, 49]. However, such an agent still falls short on physical interaction with objects, so growing line of work on agent-orchestrated robot manipulation integrates learned visuomotor policy, typically vision-language-action (VLA) model, into the agent framework [7, 10, 15, 21, 35, 43, 51, 52]. In these systems, the agent decides when to call the policy and how to instruct the policy, and the interface between the agent and the policy becomes the main bottleneck [14]. Most existing attempts address this bottleneck from the agent side by adding verification and memory around frozen policy [15, 32, 43]. In this paper, we address this bottleneck from the policy side: we train the policy so that its handoff boundary is wide and explicit to the agent, and then expand this boundary as the system runs. Robot skill learning. Rather than learning one policy for the whole task, long line of work decomposes tasks into reusable skills and composes them at run time [24, 25, 28, 29, 39]. With generalist VLA policies [24, 20, 30], these skills are now fine-tuned from, or prompted out of, one shared model [11, 13, 44, 47, 48]. Each such skill can start only from certain states, which are classically modeled as the initiation set of an option [38] and are learned so that skills can be chained [22]. In this paper, the contact segments on which we fine-tune the policy in boundary-explicit training can also be viewed as such skills, but we do so Agent-orchestrated robot manipulation. Here, we use general-purpose agent that orchestrates learned visuomotor policy πθ to solve the manipulation task. The agent calls tools in loop, where the k-th call ck A( ℓ, M, hk) is conditioned on the instruction, memory and the history hk of earlier calls. Each call either perceives the scene, reads or writes the memory, or controls the robot through motion tools, such as planner that reaches an endeffector target x, or through the policy πθ, which runs with short command for chunks of actions. After each call, the agent receives the new observation, and this loop continues until the agent finishes the task or budget of calls is spent. Following Harness VLA [51], the agent first explores each task and writes what it learns into the memory , which stays fixed at evaluation. Handoff boundary. When the agent calls the policy, it hands over control of the robot to the policy, and we refer to this transfer as handoff. handoff is reliable only if the agent hands over in state from which the policy can complete its command. Formally, we define the handoff boundary Bϵ(πθ, u) as the set of observations from which the policy completes command with probability at least 1 ϵ: Bϵ(πθ, u) = { : Pθ(o, u) 1 ϵ } , (1) where Pθ(o, u) is the probability that πθ completes command when it starts from observation o. Since this probability cannot be measured for every observation, we estimate the boundary in Sec. 4.4 from the success rate of the policy at increasing distances from its training trajectories. 3.2. Boundary-explicit training The handoff boundary Bϵ(πθ, u) in Eq. (1) is mainly set by the data on which the policy is trained. whole-task policy, which is trained on complete demonstrations of entire tasks, often has handoff boundary that is narrow and hard to describe in the middle of task. Data collection and policy training. To address this problem, we first define the roles of the agent and the policy: the policy handles only the contact segments of each task, in which the robot physically interacts with objects, and the agent does the rest. The handoff boundary therefore lies near the graspable points of the target object. We then collect demonstrations of contact segments from diverse start poses within this region to widen the boundary, as shown in the data-collection scene of Fig. 3a. Each demonstration in the resulting object-interaction data D0 pairs command u, such as Pick up the stapler with the left arm, with sequence of observationaction pairs (ot, at). For example, on RoboTwin 2.0, we collect demonstrations of 147 subtasks across the 50 tasks, and further details of D0 are provided in Appendix B. We fine-tune pretrained policy, π0.5 [2], on D0 with end-effector poses as the action representation, which matches the end-effector targets that the Figure 2. Illustration of agent-orchestrated robot manipulation, with the components of our method highlighted in color. to give the policy an explicit handoff boundary, so that the agent knows when and where to hand over. Self-improving robot systems. Beyond fixed memory, robot system can keep improving after deployment. Early work rewrites the agents memory from failures [36, 39]. More recently, robot agents discover new skills [24, 28], curate their own executions into training data [6, 26, 42], and fine-tune the policy from model-guided exploration [19, 37, 40]. Closest to our work, Robo-COP fine-tunes VLA policy on its own executions to fix recurring failures and revises the agents memory after each update [50]. In this paper, we retrain the policy on the systems successful rollouts and let the agent re-explore each task with the retrained policy, so that the agent hands over earlier and needs fewer language-model calls. 3. Method In this paper, we study agent-orchestrated robot manipulation, which combines general-purpose agent, equipped with system prompt, memory and tools, with learned visuomotor policy to solve robot manipulation tasks, as shown in Fig. 2. We consider this paradigm better choice than letting the agent control the robot directly, which we examine in an early exploratory study (Appendix G). Boundary-Aware Policy Learning improves this system through the handoff between the agent and the policy: boundary-explicit training (Sec. 3.2) makes the handoff reliable, and boundary-expanding self-improvement (Sec. 3.3) lets the agent hand over earlier. 3.1. Preliminaries Task setup. In robot manipulation task, robot acts in an environment to follow language instruction ℓ. At each control step t, the robot provides an observation ot with RGB images, depth maps and the proprioceptive state, and policy Π outputs an action at Π( ot, ℓ). The robot executes at, which changes the environment, and this loop repeats until the task is completed. Figure 3. Illustration of Boundary-Aware Policy Learning. (a) Boundary-Explicit Training collects contact-segment demonstrations D0 from diverse start poses near the target object and fine-tunes the policy on these segments. simple handoff protocol then guides (b) Boundary-Expanding the agent to enter the policys reliable region, invoke it for one contact segment, and verify the outcome. Self-Improvement collects successful system rollouts, removes suboptimal behaviors through curation, and re-executes the tasks to construct D1. Retraining the policy on D0 D1 expands its handoff boundary toward earlier task stages, enabling earlier handoffs with fewer language-model calls. agent specifies. The resulting policy thus has wide and explicit handoff boundary. such as repeated adjustments of the arm pose and retries after failed policy call. Handoff protocol. The handoff protocol describes this boundary to the agent as rules in its prompt, which restate how the start poses of grasp were sampled (8 to 12 cm above the grasp point) and how to hand over within the boundary. Since the boundary is explicit, these rules need no example images or task-specific descriptions, and the same protocol applies to every task. Under these rules, the agent calls the policy only for contact segment, with short command that names the segment. Before each call, the agent locates the target object with its perception tools and moves the gripper into the boundary with one planner motion. The agent then runs the policy for at most four chunks, so that the call stays short enough to check. After the call, the agent checks the result in fresh observations and takes over again. If the contact segment has failed, the agent observes the scene again and moves the gripper back into the boundary before the next call. The bottom of Fig. 3a shows one such call, from finding the object to the check. 3.3. Boundary-expanding self-improvement With boundary-explicit the agent hands over training, only the contact segments and completes the rest of each task through many slow and costly language-model calls. Boundary-expanding self-improvement reduces these calls by expanding the handoff boundary toward earlier stages of each task, so that the agent can hand over earlier. The training data for this expansion come from the system itself, since its successful rollouts of entire tasks match its own distribution. However, these rollouts should not be imitated directly, because they contain suboptimal segments, Data curation. To remove these segments, we use data curation pipeline of two steps. curation agent first labels every segment of rollout as useful or suboptimal and keeps the useful segments as reference. Since directly removing the suboptimal segments would leave abrupt jumps in the robot state between the remaining segments, we then let the agent re-execute the task in the same scene following this reference and record the re-executed rollouts as the final system rollout data D1, as shown at the top of Fig. 3b. Retraining and re-exploration. We retrain the policy on D0 and D1 together, and the retrained parameters θ minimize its training loss over both datasets: θ = arg min θ E(ot,at,g)D0D1 L(cid:0)πθ( ot, g), at (cid:1), (2) where the language input is the command of contact segment in D0 or the instruction ℓ of whole task in D1. The policy thus learns to complete whole task from the instruction while keeping its ability to perform single contact segment from command. The whole-task rollouts in D1 extend the handoff boundary to earlier stages of each task, so that the agent can hand over before the gripper reaches the target object. Since D1 records each task in the way the agent orchestrates it, its contact segments also start inside the boundary learned in Sec. 3.2 and thus agree with D0, so the agent can still hand over in the middle of task. To adapt to the retrained policy, we update the handoff protocol to describe the expanded boundary, and the agent reexplores each task and updates its memory , which again stays fixed at evaluation. Under the updated protocol, the agent first hands over the whole task from the initial pose and falls back to contact-segment calls when the progress stalls or step fails. As result, the agent needs fewer language-model calls, as the bottom of Fig. 3b illustrates. 4. Experiments 4.1. Setup Benchmarks and protocol. We evaluate the system after boundary-explicit training on RoboTwin 2.0 [9] and RoboDojo [8]. On RoboTwin 2.0, we collect the objectinteraction data D0 with the benchmarks scripted expert and conduct agent exploration in clean scenes, then evaluate each task over 10 episodes in each of two settings: in clean scenes (C2C) and under the official randomized configuration (C2R). On RoboDojo, we evaluate on the 26 tasks in the generalization, memory and open-vocabulary subsets, with 10 episodes per task. For generalization tasks, we collect D0 and conduct agent exploration in the clean variant, then evaluate in the randomized variant, as in C2R. For memory and open-vocabulary tasks, data collection and agent exploration use seeds disjoint from evaluation. For self-improvement evaluation, we use RoboTwin 2.0, where both the collection of the system rollout data D1 and agent re-exploration take place in randomized scenes. Since this randomized configuration is now used during self-improvement, we define two evaluation settings to assess generalization. The easy setting uses unseen seeds of the same randomized configuration. The hard setting also uses unseen seeds, replaces the textures and the distractor objects with assets imported from RoboDojo and changes the lighting, none of which appear during training or exploration. In both settings, we report the success rate together with the number of language-model calls, the API cost and the time per episode. Baselines. We compare our method with representative baselines for end-to-end policy execution and agentbased robot control. As an end-to-end learned policy baseline, we fine-tune π0.5 [2] on the official whole-task demonstrations in clean scenes together with D0, so that it learns from the same contact segments as our policy, and evaluate it end to end. AGP [18] represents agents with runtime programming, in which the agent writes and revises programs for perception and robot control during execution. ORA [46] represents agents with predefined perception and motion tools, and neither AGP nor ORA uses learned policy. Harness VLA [51] represents agents that orchestrate learned policy. Following its official setting, we equip it with LingBot-VLA [41], whole-task policy fine-tuned on RoboTwin 2.0 and released with Harness VLA. Main results An explicit handoff boundary brings large gains on both benchmarks. We compare the system after boundaryexplicit training with the baselines in Tab. 1, which leads to two conclusions. First, an explicit handoff boundary brings large gains even over Harness VLA, which also orchestrates learned policy: our system is 26.4 percentage points higher on RoboTwin 2.0 under the official randomized configuration (C2R) and 28.4 percentage points higher on average on RoboDojo. Second, handing over only the contact segments makes the system less sensitive to scene randomization. whole-task policy can complete most tasks in clean scenes (C2C), where π0.5 alone reaches 85.8% and Harness VLA reaches 96.0%, but randomization lowers them to 40.0% and 72.0%, whereas the success rate of our system does not drop. The agent and the policy complement each other. Taking closer look at the subsets of RoboDojo, we find two interesting observations. First, memory and open-vocabulary tasks rely on the agent: the whole-task policy π0.5 rarely succeeds, whereas AGP, an agent without learned policy, performs much better on both. Second, AGP achieves only 10.0% on the generalization subset, since its tasks test generalization to new scenes through diverse physical interactions with objects. By combining the two, our system leads in all three subsets, with the agent handling task-level reasoning and orchestration and the policy providing closedloop control for physical interaction with objects. Boundary analysis Self-improvement makes the system faster and cheaper to run. To evaluate boundary-expanding self-improvement, we compare the system before and after this stage on all 50 tasks of RoboTwin 2.0 in the easy and hard settings. As shown in Fig. 4a, the API cost and time per episode at execution fall by 41.3% and 37.5% on average, while the success rate does not drop. These savings come from about 40% fewer language-model calls, since the agent now hands over to the retrained policy earlier in each task. We further conduct second round of self-improvement on 30 randomly selected tasks with new system rollout data D2. As shown in Fig. 4b, this round lowers the API cost and time per episode by further 18% to 27%, while the success rate stays above 98% in both settings, which suggests that self-improvement can be repeated as the system runs. Details about the cost of data collection are provided in Appendix C. Curated system rollouts are as effective as expert demonstrations. We then ask whether curated system rollouts can replace expert demonstrations for training policy to complete whole tasks. We therefore train two policies on the same amount of data from randomized scenes, one on curated system rollouts and one on official expert demonstrations, and test both without the agent in the easy and hard settings. The two policies achieve similar success rates (see Appendix C), within 3.0 percentage points in each setting. This suggests that our system can also collect training data for visuomotor policies, as an alternative to teleoperation or scripted motion planning. To understand where the gains of boundary-explicit training come from, we analyze the handoff boundary in our system and in Harness VLA, which leads to three key findings. Key Finding 1: The policy is reliable near its training data. To assess how our policy performs inside its handoff boundary, we evaluate it on the 147 subtasks of D0 after boundary-explicit training and report the success rates in Fig. 5a. Starting from training poses, the policy reaches 93.2% in clean scenes and 89.8% in randomized scenes, so it generalizes well across scene appearance. Furthermore, starting from new poses, namely held-out start poses and their shifts by up to 4 cm, its success rate stays high at 83.7%. Appendix details the evaluation settings. Overall, the policy is robust to pose and scene changes near its training start poses, which serves as its handoff boundary for the agent. Key Finding 2: The agent hands over where the policy is reliable. To check where the agent hands over, we measure the distance from the gripper at each first handoff to the training trajectories of the policy, and group the trials of the policy from new poses by the same distance. As shown in Fig. 5b, 91.1% of the first handoffs lie within 40 mm, where the policy succeeds in at least 82.2% of trials. Only 6.1% of the first handoffs lie beyond 60 mm, where the policy still succeeds in 59.1% of trials. Fig. 5c further shows that the first handoffs in four tasks lie among the training trajectories. Taken together, these results show that, under the handoff protocol, the agent mostly hands over within the handoff boundary of the policy. Qualitative analysis In Fig. 7, we visualize the complete execution of placing cup on coaster by Harness VLA and by our system before and after self-improvement and make three observations. Harness VLA tends to hand over the whole task at the start and fails after several attempts. As shown in Fig. 7a, the agent of Harness VLA calls the whole-task policy from the initial pose, as it does in almost all episodes (Key FindIn this scene, unseen in training, the ing 3 in Sec. 4.4). policy fails to grasp the cup and knocks it off the table, so the gripper reaches the coaster empty. With the cup off the table, two further whole-task calls also fail, and the agent gives up. After boundary-explicit training, the agent hands over only the contact segment. As shown in Fig. 7b, the agent of our system first moves the gripper above the cup with one planner motion, so that the policy starts inside its handoff boundary. The agent then hands over only the grasp with the short command Pick up the cup with the left arm, and the policy lifts the cup within two chunks. The agent carries and places the cup itself with three more planner motions and release, and the episode succeeds. After self-improvement, the retrained policy performs the whole task in the same steps as the system. As shown in Fig. 7c, the agent calls the retrained policy with the task instruction from the initial pose. The policy then approaches, grasps, carries and places the cup in single call, following the same steps as the whole system in Fig. 7b. This makes the system cheaper and faster, with only 4 language-model calls and 135 in this episode. Failure cases of our system are shown in Appendix E. 5. Conclusion We presented Boundary-Aware Policy Learning, which enables more reliable agentpolicy coordination in agentorchestrated robot manipulation. Boundary-Explicit Training fine-tunes the policy only on contact segments with diverse start poses, so that short handoff protocol can describe its wide and explicit handoff boundary to the agent. Boundary-Expanding Self-Improvement then retrains the policy on the systems own curated rollouts, so that the boundary extends to earlier stages of each task. With boundary-explicit training alone, the system outperforms the strongest baseline by more than 26 percentage points in randomized scenes of RoboTwin 2.0 and on RoboDojo, and self-improvement further reduces the API cost and time per episode by 41.3% and 37.5% on average without loss in success rate. These results suggest that an orchestrated system improves most when the boundary between the agent and the policy is made explicit and expanded over time. Limitations and future work. First, data curation discards the suboptimal segments of each rollout, which DAgger [31] or offline reinforcement learning [23] may turn into training data on how the system recovers from mistakes. Second, the handoff protocol describes the boundary only by rules, and policy that outputs confidence for the current state, like SayCan [1], may let the agent check each handoff position.

sections.title: Appendix
sections.content: The appendix is organized as follows. Experimental Setup (Appendix A): the benchmarks and the evaluation protocol, the tools, observations and memory of the agent, and the baselines. Details of Boundary-Explicit Training (Appendix B): the object-interaction data D0 and its subtasks on both benchmarks, the training of our policy, and the handoff protocol in the prompt of the agent. Details of Boundary-Expanding Self-Improvement (Appendix C): the data curation pipeline, retraining and reexploration, the cost of data collection, the easy and hard evaluation settings, the numbers behind Fig. 4, and the comparison of policies trained on curated system rollouts and on expert demonstrations. Details of the Boundary Analysis (Appendix D): the evaluation of our policy on the 147 subtasks, the distance to the training trajectories, and the analysis of Harness VLA. Additional Results (Appendix E): the task subset of the ablations, the scores on RoboDojo, the failure cases of our system, and first attempt to deploy our system on real robot (Sec. E.2). Prompt and Memory (Appendix F): the evaluation prompt of the agent after boundary-explicit training, shown as the sections that we add for the handoff protocol and the sections kept from Harness VLA, and two entries of its memory. Closer Look at Agent-Direct Control (Appendix G): an early exploratory study of agents that control the robot directly, which reports what the agent can and cannot do and discusses future directions. A. Experimental Setup This section details the setup of the experiments in Sec. 4: the benchmarks and the evaluation protocol, the agent with its tools, observations and memory, and the baselines. Benchmarks. RoboTwin 2.0 [9] contains 50 tasks on dual-arm robot. Compared with its clean configuration, the official randomized configuration changes the background textures, scatters distractor objects on the table, randomizes the lighting and lowers the table by random height, as Fig. S1 illustrates. On RoboDojo [8], we use the 26 tasks of the generalization, memory and open-vocabulary subsets listed in Tab. S1, and exclude the long-horizon and precision subsets, on which training policy rarely succeeds. Each generalization task has clean variant and randomized variant, which replaces the main objects with unseen instances and adds distractor objects in most tasks. Table S1. The 26 RoboDojo tasks used in our evaluation. Each generalization task is evaluated in its randomized variant. Subset Tasks Task names Generalization 12 Memory Open-vocabulary 6 8 stack bowls, push T, pack objects into box, fold clothes, hang mugs, sweep blocks, pour liquid into cup, make toast, arrange largest number, sort nesting dolls by size, store laptop and headphones, stack blocks cover blocks, match and pick from conveyor, swap blocks, swap T, press by number, imitate sorting sequence align blocks, general pickup, solve equation, stack blocks by language, classify objects by language, pick from conveyor by image, store tools in toolbox, pour by language Exploration and evaluation protocol. On RoboTwin 2.0, exploration follows Harness VLA [51]: each task is explored in clean scene in up to three agent sessions with up to five attempts each, the scene is reset before every attempt, and every new session reads the failure records of the previous sessions. The exploration of task stops at its first success, and the notes of all tasks are then merged into one memory, which stays frozen during evaluation. Our system and every baseline are evaluated on 10 different scene seeds per task, each baseline in its own configuration. In the main results, an episode of our system is limited to 100 language-model calls and 5,000 s, and the native predicate of the benchmark judges success. The easy and hard settings of self-improvement are described in Appendix C. Figure S1. Clean, randomized and hard scenes. Head-camera images at the start of an episode for three tasks. The randomized scene is built with the official randomized configuration, and the hard setting (Appendix C) builds the same scene with textures, distractor objects and lighting that do not occur during data collection or exploration. The clean scene shows another layout of the same task. Agent and tools. The agent is Claude Opus 5.5 with high reasoning effort and acts only through registered tools, the main ones of which are listed in Tab. S2, since we disable the built-in tools of the agent framework, such as the shell. Perception tools return camera images, the image location of named object from SAM 3 [5] and the world coordinates of image pixels, and motion tools move one end effector to pose through the benchmarks motion planner, rotate wrist or set gripper. The policy tool takes command and number of chunks, which the tool limits to at most four after boundary-explicit training and to at most 24 after self-improvement (Appendix C). Each chunk consists of 50 actions, which specify the absolute endeffector poses and gripper commands of both arms and are executed for 40 ms each. The policy observes the scene again before every chunk, and the call stops as soon as the native predicate reports success. The reset tool exists only during exploration. Observations and success signal. The agent and the policy observe the scene through the same three RGB cameras, head camera and two wrist cameras, which also record D0. These cameras render 640 480 images with wider vertical fields of view than the benchmarks default cameras, namely 55 at the head and 85 at the wrists. After every tool call that changes the robot state, the agent receives the three images together with the proprioception, which reports the joint positions, the end-effector poses of both arms and the gripper openings. Depth is never shown to the agent as an image, and the agent instead reads the world coordinates of selected pixels or of an image region. Besides these observations, the agent receives the binary success flag of the benchmarks native predicate, which an operator or success detector would provide on real robot. The tool that ends an episode reports the result of this predicate, so the agent cannot declare success by itself. Simulator state such as object poses or contacts reaches neither the agent nor the policy, and the policy does not see the success flag either. Memory. The memory has three layers: global notes that apply to all tasks, task-family notes, and for every task record of its successful exploration attempt. This record contains the plan of the attempt and its recipe, the sequence of state-changing commands with their arguments, with an example in Appendix F. During exploration, the prompt adds the memory-writing Table S2. Main tools available to the agent after boundary-explicit training. Every tool that changes the robot state returns fresh observation with the robot state and the images of the head camera and the two wrist cameras. Depth is never returned as an image, and the agent reads the world coordinates of chosen pixels through the two depth-query tools. At evaluation, the frozen memory is read-only, and the prompt asks the agent to use the recipe as plan for the order and type of actions, not as coordinates to replay. Baselines. On RoboTwin 2.0, the whole-task policy π0.5 [2] uses the model and optimization settings of our policy (Appendix B), is fine-tuned on D0 together with 2,650 official whole-task demonstrations in clean scenes (53 per task), and runs end to end from the task instruction. On RoboDojo, π0.5 is fine-tuned on the official demonstrations, which contain none of the open-vocabulary tasks. AGP [18] observes the scene only through RGB images and writes programs for perception and robot control at run time, while ORA [46], which we run with its official implementation, gives the agent predefined perception and motion tools. Details of Boundary-Expanding Self-Improvement This section gives the details of boundary-expanding self-improvement, which Sec. 3.3 describes and Sec. 4.3 evaluates. Data curation. We collect the system rollouts on RoboTwin 2.0 with the system after boundary-explicit training under the official randomized configuration and keep only the successful rollouts. curation agent, which is language model, then reads each rollout through its tool calls with their arguments and results, the gripper state from proprioception and headcamera images taken at key moments of the rollout, such as after each grasp and release. Apart from the success flag, no simulator state such as object poses reaches the curation agent. For every grasp in the rollout, the curation agent decides whether the grasp is part of the solution that finally succeeds or belongs to failed or repeated attempt, and marks the calls that only adjust the arm pose. The suboptimal segments are these failed and repeated attempts and pose adjustments. These segments are removed, and the remaining calls form the reference in their original order. Fixed rules then merge repeated calls, may combine an earlier grasp with the transport and placement of the final attempt, and restore or add free move where the removal leaves large gap between kept poses. Re-execution and acceptance. rollout without suboptimal segments is kept as it is, and every other rollout is re-executed. For re-execution, the scene is reset to its initial state, and the agent follows the reference step by step while the policy is called online, with up to three attempts. re-executed rollout enters D1 only if the task succeeds, the executed steps follow the order of the reference and no grasp is empty. Rollouts that are unusually long, or in which an object that the robot did not touch moves, are also discarded. The latter check reads object poses after collection and only filters the data: no simulator state reaches the agent, the curation agent or the policy. After curation, D1 contains 30 rollouts per task, or 1,500 in total. Retraining and re-exploration. We retrain the policy from the base checkpoint of π0.5 on D0 and D1 for 2,000 steps with the other settings of Tab. S6. Besides the whole-task rollouts, the contact segments of the system rollouts also serve as training samples with their commands u. After retraining, the handoff protocol is updated to describe the expanded boundary. The agent first calls the policy from the initial pose with the task instruction, and one call may now run up to 24 chunks. If the task is unfinished after this call, the agent calls the policy again with the task instruction while the task progresses. When the progress stalls or step fails, the agent continues as in the first stage and hands over the remaining contact segments with their commands. With this protocol, the agent re-explores each task in randomized scenes from the memory of the first stage and revises this memory, which is then frozen for evaluation. The second round on the 30-task subset (Appendix E) repeats these steps: we collect D2 in the same way, with 30 rollouts per task, retrain the policy on D0, D1 and D2, and let the agent re-explore each task. Details of the Boundary Analysis This section details the evaluation settings and the measurements behind the boundary analysis in Sec. 4.4. Policy evaluation on the 147 subtasks. We run our policy alone, without the agent, on the 147 subtasks of D0 from five start poses per subtask in each of three settings, which gives 735 trials per setting. The first two settings start from training poses, the start poses of training demonstrations, in clean scenes and in randomized scenes. The third setting starts from new poses in randomized scenes: the start pose of the validation demonstration of each subtask (Appendix B), whose scene differs from those of the training demonstrations, and four shifts of this pose by 1 to 4 cm, one in each horizontal direction. Success in each trial is judged by predicate of the subtask that reads the simulator state. This predicate is used only in this evaluation, and neither the agent nor the policy has access to it. Distance to the training trajectories. The distance in Key Finding 2 is measured in the frame of the target object, whose pose comes from the simulator and serves only for this offline analysis. In this frame, the distance of gripper position to the training trajectories is its nearest distance to the gripper positions of the training demonstrations of the same subtask and arm before contact, where contact begins when the gripper starts to close or, for skills without grasp, at the closest approach to the object. This distance covers only the position of the gripper, not its orientation. In Fig. 5b and c, we use the first policy calls in the C2R evaluation episodes of our system in Tab. 1. The success rate of the policy in Fig. 5b is computed over the trials from new poses above, with the distance taken at the start pose, and covers only the subtasks that start before grasp. We deploy our system on real dual-arm robot with two dexterous hands, head camera and wrist camera on each arm. The task is to put pear and an orange into white bowl, and the instruction is Put the fruits on the table into the white bowl. For boundary-explicit training, we collect 20 teleoperated demonstrations of picking up each fruit in clean scene, which contains only the two fruits and the bowl. As in simulation, each demonstration records only the interaction with the object, from hand pose near the fruit until the fruit is lifted. These start poses vary around the fruit (Fig. S4a), so that the handoff boundary of the policy is wide. We fine-tune π0.5 on the 40 demonstrations. The test scene differs from this clean scene, with several distractor objects and different tablecloth (Fig. S4b). The agent is the same as in simulation, and its tools observe the scene, segment objects with SAM3, move hand to target pose, open hand and call the policy. Results. Figure S4 shows one episode. The agent first reads the instruction, segments the head-camera image, and locates the pear on the left and the orange on the right (Fig. S4b). It then plans to pick up each fruit with the hand on the same side. For the pear, the agent moves the left hand to start pose near the fruit and hands over to our policy, which grasps and lifts the pear (Fig. S4c). The agent then carries the pear above the bowl and opens the hand, and it repeats these steps for the orange with the right hand. Both fruits end in the bowl, and the task is completed. This first attempt covers single task, and we leave quantitative evaluation on real robots to future work. Outlook. In early attempts, we let the agent grasp the fruits by itself with commands that close the hand, and none of these attempts succeeded. This suggests that the agent alone still has long way to go on tasks with dexterous hands, and we attribute this to two reasons. First, dexterous hand has many degrees of freedom, which are hard to coordinate through discrete commands. Second, the interaction between the fingers and the object is problem of contact dynamics. The fingers must respond to the contact continuously, while the agent senses contact only indirectly and acts at far lower rate (Sec. G.3). Handing the grasp to learned policy compensates for part of this weakness. However, policy that only grasps is not enough, as the value of dexterous hand lies in adjusting the object within the hand during the task. What capabilities learned policy should have in dexterous manipulation, and how the agent should steer it, are therefore directions worth exploring. Figure S4. Closer Look at Agent-Direct Control This section reports the study behind statement in Sec. 1: an agent built on general-purpose multimodal model is strong at task-level decisions and generalizes across layouts and instructions, but it executes contact poorly. Before building our system, we let such an agent control dual-arm robot directly on RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboDojo without any robot training, which we call agent-direct control, and we re-examine every failed trial. Sec. G.1 describes the setup, Sec. G.2 and Sec. G.3 report what the agent does well and where it falls short, and Sec. G.4 discusses the research directions that follow. G.1. Setup Agent and interface. The agent is Claude Opus 5.5 with xhigh reasoning effort, the level between the high and max efforts in Tab. 2, and we give it no robot training data, no demonstrations and no memory between trials. It observes RGB images from the wrist cameras and from fixed cameras with known poses, together with the proprioceptive state, but no depth, table height or object poses. It acts through 11 low-level commands, such as capturing images, reading the robot state, moving an end effector or the joints and opening or closing gripper, and the command counts below include only those that capture images or move the robot. Discussion and Future Directions Agent-direct control replaces robot data with reasoning at run time. In our study, each strength of this choice comes with cost, and each pair raises research direction. Agent-direct control is general but not dexterous. Reasoning lets the agent solve new tasks without training but does not make physical interaction with objects precise, which raises the question of how to combine reasoning with learned control. The missing ability can be trained into the language model, built into perception and motion tools, or handed over to learned policy. The third route must say where the boundary between the agent and the policy lies and how the agent knows it. Agent-direct control is deliberate but slow. Observing and reasoning between commands lets the agent recover and check its own work, but it also takes most of the time of trial. In simulation, the scene waits while the agent reasons, whereas real scene may keep changing. This raises the question of where reasoning should be spent, that is, which decisions need the language model and which do not. Agent-direct control needs no training but does not learn from experience by itself. In our study, the agent keeps no memory between trials, so it solves each task as if for the first time. This raises the question of how experience becomes ability: whether it belongs in memory, in reusable programs or in the weights of policy, and whether the agent can become source of robot data. Experience can also be trained into the agent itself: just as general agents have internalized computer use through large-scale post-training with reinforcement learning, we believe that they can internalize robot control from their experience on robots. Agent-direct control follows language, but existing benchmarks do not evaluate it well. The two benchmarks in this study, like most existing ones, are designed for policies that learn from demonstrations, and our study meets four gaps when they evaluate an agent. First, their success checks contain conventions that demonstrations convey but the instruction does not state, as the unstated numeric criteria in Fig. S5 show. Second, the simulation waits while the agent reasons, and the benchmarks count neither time nor cost. Third, binary success signal cannot separate an instruction that the agent misunderstands from one that it fails to execute. Fourth, the benchmarks do not specify how many attempts the agent may make, what it may remember or whether it sees the success signal. Benchmarks designed for agentic robot manipulation may close these gaps by stating the required final state in the instruction and by fixing the time limit and the memory rules. Among the four research directions above, this paper mainly addresses the first, how to combine reasoning with learned control, and hands physical interaction with objects over to learned policy. Its key idea is to define and expand the handoff boundary between the agent and the policy through training (Sec. 3.2 and Sec. 3.3). In summary, general agent already provides the task-level decisions of manipulation without robot training, and the open problems are how to combine it with learned control, where to spend its reasoning, how to turn its experience into ability and how to evaluate it.
